```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(semTests)
```

## What do you want to test?

Suppose a factor model has two loadings, `a` and `b`, and we want to test
whether they are equal. We can examine their estimated difference (Wald),
examine the score after imposing equality (score), or compare the fitting
criteria with and without equality (criterion difference).

These are tests of a **restriction within a model**. Testing whether the
whole model fits the population moments exactly is a separate question.

| Question | Function | Fits needed |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Does the whole model fit exactly? | `score_test()` | The proposed model |
| Are the two loadings equal? | `wald_test()` | The unrestricted model |
| Can the equality restriction be released? | `score_test_nested()` | The restricted model and an alternative specification |
| Does equality leave the population minimum criterion unchanged? | `criterion_test_nested()` | Both models |

We first work through the equality restriction using complete continuous data.
The examples specify their inference settings explicitly; alternative settings
are explained below.

## One restriction, three tests

```{r models, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.alt="Two one-factor models with four indicators. The unrestricted model has loadings a and b on x2 and x3; the restricted model uses the same loading on both paths.", fig.cap="The same factor model before and after imposing equality. Blue paths identify the restriction. Residuals are uncorrelated; intercepts and variances are omitted from the drawing."}
knitr::include_graphics(if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  "figures/score-wald-models.pdf"
} else {
  "figures/score-wald-models.svg"
})
```

The first loading is fixed to 1 in both models, so their factor scales agree.
The loadings of `x2` and `x3` are labelled `a` and `b`. Our null is `a - b = 0`;
the loading of `x4`, variances, and intercepts remain free in both models.

```{r fits}
d <- lavaan::HolzingerSwineford1939
model <- "f =~ x1 + a*x2 + b*x3 + x4"
fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, d, meanstructure = TRUE)
restricted <- lavaan::cfa(paste(model, "a == b", sep = "\n"),
                          d, meanstructure = TRUE)
lavaan::coef(fit)[c("a", "b")]
```

### Wald: evaluate the estimated difference

Wald uses the unrestricted estimates and their sampling covariance. The row
matrix `R` encodes `a - b`: its columns follow `lavaan::coef(fit)`, with 1 for
`a`, -1 for `b`, and zero elsewhere. The right-hand side is zero by default.

```{r wald}
R <- matrix(0, 1, length(lavaan::coef(fit)))
R[1, match(c("a", "b"), names(lavaan::coef(fit)))] <- c(1, -1)
w <- wald_test(fit, R, vcov = "sandwich",
               curvature = "observed", score_covariance = "centered",
               hypothesis = "a = b", keep = TRUE)
w
```

This measures the squared estimated loading difference relative to its
sampling variance. The sandwich covariance accounts for the variability of
the estimating equations; its ingredients are explained below.

### Score: evaluate the restricted fit

The score test starts where `a = b` has been imposed. It measures the evidence
for moving away from equality, after accounting for the other free parameters.
This adjustment for the other parameters is what **profile** means here.

```{r score}
profile <- score_test_nested(restricted, fit,
                             metric = "sandwich",
                             curvature = "observed", score_covariance = "centered",
                             hypothesis = "a = b", keep = TRUE)
profile
```

Here `metric = "sandwich"` scales the adjusted score by its own covariance,
giving a chi-square reference. Only the restricted fit needs to be optimized.
We reuse `fit` to supply the alternative parameterization; an unfitted template
would also work:

```{r template, eval=FALSE}
template <- lavaan::cfa(model, d, meanstructure = TRUE, do.fit = FALSE)
score_test_nested(restricted, template, metric = "sandwich",
                  curvature = "observed", score_covariance = "centered")
```

Nested models must use the same data, criterion, factor scaling, and aligned
parameterization. Keeping the same model syntax and adding an equality
constraint, as above, makes that relationship explicit.

### Criterion difference: compare both fits

This test uses the increase in the fitted criterion caused by equality. Both
models must be optimized. The reference distribution is calculated at the
restricted fit.

```{r criterion}
criterion <- criterion_test_nested(restricted, fit,
                                    curvature = "observed", score_covariance = "centered",
                                    hypothesis = "a = b")
criterion
```

For this regular nested comparison, the null says the population minimum
criterion is unchanged by the restriction. Under the common-target assumptions
discussed below, that is the same equality restriction addressed by score and
Wald. Their sample statistics and p-values need not coincide.

```{r comparison, echo=FALSE}
comparison <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Wald", "Score", "Criterion difference"),
  Statistic = c(w$statistic, profile$statistic, criterion$statistic),
  `p-value` = c(w$p_value, profile$p_value, criterion$p_value),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 4)
```

For example, the Wald p-value is `r format.pval(w$p_value, digits = 3)`.
At a 5% threshold, this test
`r if (w$p_value < .05) "rejects equality of the two loadings" else "does not reject equality of the two loadings"`.
Failure to reject would not establish equality, and none of these restriction
tests establishes that the whole factor model fits exactly.

## What if the factor model is misspecified?

A model can fail to reproduce the population moments even at its best-fitting
parameter value. That value is the **pseudo-parameter**: the minimizer of the
population fitting criterion. Under structural misspecification, `a = b`
refers to its two loadings, rather than to parameters of a true factor model.
The target can depend on the fitting criterion.

For nested inference, we require a shared criterion and, under the null, a
common population minimizer in the restricted model. We also need the usual
local regularity conditions, including identification and suitable curvature.
A sandwich calculation does not remove those requirements.

It helps to distinguish four issues:

* **Nonnormality:** the observations need not follow a normal distribution,
  even when the model reproduces their means and covariances.
* **Structural misspecification:** the model cannot reproduce the target
  moments; restrictions concern the criterion's pseudo-parameter.
* **Missing data:** FIML uses the observed-data likelihood contributions.
  Its population target also depends on the observation process and assumptions.
* **Estimated fitting weights:** for weighted least squares, the criterion's
  weight matrix is estimated from the same data as the sample moments.

The unified treatment of restriction tests has established foundations in
Satorra (1989), and scaled and adjusted restricted tests under nonnormality
are developed in Satorra (2000). The particular missing-data, fixed-
misspecification, and estimated-weight developments used here are also the
subject of manuscripts in preparation; see the research status below.

## Curvature, score covariance, metric, and parameter covariance

The function arguments separate four ingredients:

| Argument | Meaning | Example choices |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `curvature` | How the estimating equations change with the parameters; used in nuisance adjustment and covariance construction | `"observed"`, `"expected"` |
| `score_covariance` | Sampling variability of the scores or estimating equations | `"centered"`, `"uncentered"` for likelihood scores |
| `metric` | Weighting of the adjusted score in its quadratic statistic | `"sandwich"`, `"information"` |
| `vcov` | Source of the parameter sampling covariance for Wald | `"sandwich"`, `"fitted"` |

Writing the per-observation curvature as \(H\) and the score covariance as \(J\), the sandwich
sampling covariance has the form
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)
  = \frac{1}{N}H^{-1}JH^{-\mathsf T}.
\]
With parameter constraints, this calculation takes place in the free directions.
Here **`curvature` means the derivative matrix \(H\)**, not its inverse.

For likelihood scores, `score_covariance = "uncentered"` uses raw score products, while
`"centered"` subtracts score means. `curvature = "observed"` uses full observed
curvature; `"expected"` uses the expected-information/Gauss--Newton construction.
Expected and observed curvature need not agree under structural misspecification.

For the **nested score**, `metric = "information"` uses the selected curvature for
weighting. `metric = "expected"` uses expected curvature for weighting while
retaining the selected curvature for nuisance adjustment. `metric = "sandwich"`
uses the adjusted score covariance. Thus changing the metric is a different
decision from changing the curvature.

For **Wald**, `vcov = "fitted"` uses lavaan's stored parameter covariance
(currently supported for ML/FIML). `vcov = "sandwich"` constructs it from the
selected curvature and score covariance, including fitted-mean effects.

### Choosing a p-value calibration

Each test returns a `semTests_test` object containing its statistic, hypothesis,
reference distribution, and p-value. `pvalues()` can evaluate supported
calibrations without recomputing the fitted-model ingredients.

The sandwich score above and Wald use a chi-square reference (`STD`). A score
weighted by curvature generally has a weighted chi-square reference instead:

```{r calibrations}
curvature_score <- score_test_nested(restricted, fit,
                                     metric = "information",
                                     curvature = "observed", score_covariance = "centered")
pvalues(curvature_score, c("ALL", "SB"))
```

`ALL` evaluates the weighted chi-square distribution; `SB` uses Satorra--Bentler
scaling. These are two calibrations of the same statistic. They do not change
its curvature, score covariance, or metric. The fully studentized score and Wald accept only
`STD`, since they already use a chi-square reference.

Penalized methods such as `PEBA2` are available for research comparisons with
mixture-reference tests. Availability does not establish their finite-sample
performance for each new setting.

## Global exact fit

Return now to the separate question: does the unrestricted factor model fit
the population moments exactly?

```{r global}
global <- score_test(fit, metric = "information",
                      curvature = "expected", score_covariance = "uncentered")
global
```

This compares the fitted model with saturated moments. Rejection concerns the
whole model, not specifically the equality of `a` and `b`. A robust reference
can accommodate nonnormality; it does not turn exact fit into a null allowing
fixed structural misfit.

The global score uses likelihood scores at the fitted means and covariances.
Its curvature is the **saturated-model** curvature. With the information metric,
changing to `curvature = "observed"` changes the projection but leaves the metric
as expected Fisher information. This differs from the nested score's
`metric = "information"` convention described above.

## Missing data and estimated fitting weights

The following table summarizes the new fitted-model adapters. Existing
`pvalues(fit)` and `pvalues_nested()` interfaces retain their own scope.

| Setting | Global score | Nested score and criterion | Sandwich Wald |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Complete continuous ML | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Continuous FIML | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Complete continuous GLS/WLS/DWLS/ULS | No | Yes | Yes |
| Complete all-ordered DWLS/WLS/ULS | No | Yes | Yes |

For FIML, likelihood scores are observed-data scores for each missingness
pattern. See `vignette("fiml-missing-data", package = "semTests")` for the
missing-data workflow.

For least squares, **fitting weights** are the matrix weighting discrepancies
between observed and model-implied moments. They are not sampling weights.
Their estimation can contribute to sampling variability when the structural
model is misspecified. The contribution vanishes at exact fit.

Here is the same equality restriction fitted by continuous DWLS:

```{r weights}
fit_dwls <- lavaan::cfa(model, d, meanstructure = TRUE, estimator = "DWLS",
                         ordered = FALSE)
restricted_dwls <- lavaan::cfa(paste(model, "a == b", sep = "\n"), d,
                              meanstructure = TRUE, estimator = "DWLS",
                         ordered = FALSE)
weighted_score <- score_test_nested(restricted_dwls, fit_dwls,
                                    metric = "sandwich",
                                    curvature = "observed", score_covariance = "centered",
                                    weight_effect = "estimated")
weighted_score
```

`weight_effect = "estimated"` includes the joint influence of sample moments
and estimated fitting weights. `"fixed"` treats those weights as fixed for
inference. That is a comparator, not generally the complete correction under
structural misspecification. Similarly, expected curvature alone does not generally
supply the complete correction. Least-squares adapters require centered score_covariance.

These adapters currently exclude sampling weights, clusters, nonlinear
constraints, and parameter bounds. The ordinal path requires complete,
all-ordered data with nonempty pairwise cells; it does not support mixed
indicators or pairwise missingness. See the categorical-data vignette for
background on ordinal fitting.

## Advanced use and research status

Use `keep = TRUE` to retain numerical ingredients, and inspect `$diagnostics`
and `$provenance` when checking a calculation. Stationarity and curvature
diagnostics assess the local calculation; agreement with another implementation
does not by itself establish finite-sample calibration.

The matrix interfaces support independently extracted ingredients:

* `profile_score_test_matrices()` takes scores, curvature, and score_covariance and removes
  nuisance directions, using matching summed units.
* `score_test_matrices()` takes already adjusted scores, their score_covariance, and a
  metric. It also supports explicit mean normalization with `nobs`.
* `wald_test_matrices()` takes parameter estimates, restrictions, and their
  sampling covariance. This covariance is not multiplied by sample size again.

For ordinal estimated-weight inference, the implementation differentiates the
empirical frequency functional. It retains lavaan's score-product first-stage
weight construction, but uses the estimator's actual derivative for its
influence. These can differ under first-stage misspecification. Polychoric
roots are refined before numerical differentiation; this reference calculation
can be slow with many distinct response patterns.

Two ongoing manuscript projects provide the context for the additional
constructions: a manuscript on FIML goodness-of-fit inference, and a manuscript
on inference under structural misspecification, including estimated fitting
weights. Both are **in preparation**; formal bibliographic entries are
pending. The package examples
illustrate the interface and targets, rather than claiming finite-sample
validity for every combination of settings.

## References

Satorra, A. (2000). Scaled and adjusted restricted tests in multi-sample analysis
of moment structures. In R. D. H. Heijmans, D. S. G. Pollock, & A. Satorra
(Eds.), *Innovations in Multivariate Statistical Analysis* (pp. 233--247).
Kluwer Academic Publishers. <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4615-4603-0_17>.
